account: University researchers worked with Flint’s service-line replacement program from summer 2016. ActiveRemediation used property records and confirmed pipe materials to recommend inspections. Its held-out prediction accuracy was 91.6%. The researchers reported that the program had replaced hazardous lines at 4,419 homes by September 2017. A separate simulation estimated savings of about US$622 per replacement. Independent reporting later documented a decline in inspection success after the contractor changed its approach, alongside changes in geography and policy. A March 2019 court order required prioritization using the model’s address lists. The field evidence does not isolate the model’s effect on residents’ health or realized expenditure.

ai_role.statement: Predictions helped officials prioritize inspections and replacements. The field comparison also involved changes in geography and policy, so it does not isolate the model’s contribution. The monetary saving came from simulation.

value.text: Crews inspected pipes and recorded their materials. Researchers used those results to update predictions and recommend further inspections.

purpose: The model and active-learning rules were built to predict which Flint homes had lead or galvanized service lines and to direct inspections and replacements. The improved hit rate was the intended use.

ratings.reason: Residents benefited from identification and replacement of hazardous service lines, without a measured health effect attributable to the model.
The program gained a measured capability to predict pipe materials and prioritize work.
Flint replaced hazardous service lines at thousands of homes, with predictions helping prioritize inspections.

must_hold: Official use of the predictions alongside local needs
produced_by: Digitized parcel records and confirmed pipe materials

Researchers, officials, and contractors who shared information
